nameStory: Canadian buffalo-berry gets its name from its northern range and its historical importance to buffalo-hunting peoples of the Great Plains, who used these nutritious berries as a vital food source. The 'buffalo' connection comes from the berries often being mixed with dried buffalo meat to make pemmican, a high-energy trail food that could last for months.
description: Canadian buffalo-berry is a hardy deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall with a dense, spreading form. This member of the oleaster family has distinctive silvery-scaled leaves and produces small clusters of bright red or orange berries. The entire plant has a somewhat dusty, silvery appearance that makes it stand out in the landscape, especially when its colorful berries ripen in late summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are silvery-green on top and distinctly silver-white underneath, with tiny scales that give them a dusty, metallic feel when rubbed between your fingers. Leaves are arranged opposite each other on the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red to orange berries cluster along the stems in late summer, each about the size of a small pea. The berries have a tart, slightly bitter taste and feel somewhat dry compared to juicier berries.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub with multiple stems branching from the base. Young branches are covered in brown scales and have a somewhat thorny appearance, though they lack true thorns.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems have grayish-brown bark with a scaly texture, while younger twigs are covered in rusty-brown scales that can be rubbed off with your finger.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellowish flowers appear in spring before the leaves fully expand, clustered along the branches. Individual flowers are only about 1/8 inch across and lack petals, making them easy to overlook.

habitat: In New England, Canadian buffalo-berry is rare and found primarily in rocky, well-drained soils of mountainous areas and exposed slopes. It prefers alkaline soils and full sun exposure, often growing alongside other hardy shrubs in harsh, windswept locations. You're most likely to encounter it in the northern mountains of Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine.

seasonality.spring: Small yellowish flowers appear in April to May before leaves fully expand. New silvery leaves emerge, creating a striking contrast with the darker winter stems.
seasonality.summer: Foliage reaches full size, showing distinctive silvery undersides. Tiny green berries begin forming and gradually swell through mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to bright red or orange, creating the most visible season for identification. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, though fall color is usually subtle.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show scaly brown bark and distinctive opposite branching pattern. Dried berries sometimes persist on branches, and silvery leaf buds are visible.

funFact: The berries contain natural saponins (soap-like compounds) that create a frothy foam when whipped with water - indigenous peoples traditionally used this 'Indian ice cream' as both a dessert and a cleaning agent, earning it the nickname 'soapberry'!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with autumn olive, but buffalo-berry has distinctly opposite leaves (autumn olive's are alternate) and a much more silvery appearance overall. Remember: 'Buffalo's opposite, olive's alternate' - plus buffalo-berry's berries are much less juicy and more tart.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'soapberry' by some, this is completely different from the true soapberry trees (Sapindaceae family). The multiple common names including soopolallie and foamberry all reference the same foam-making property, showing how important this characteristic was to people who used the plant.
compareHints: Canadian buffalo-berry is the only Shepherdia species found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Within the oleaster family, it's distinguished from autumn olive and Russian olive by its opposite leaves, much smaller size, and distinctly different berry characteristics - buffalo-berries are drier and more tart than the juicy, sweet berries of its relatives.
